It is Meccan. It has one hundred and sixty-three letters, forty words, and eleven verses.

Al-Janazi informed us, saying: Ibn Habish related to us, saying: Abu al-Abbas al-Daqqaq informed us, saying: Abdullah ibn Rawh related to us, saying: Shababa related to us, saying: Makhlad ibn Abd al-Wahid related to us, from Ali ibn Yazid, from Zirr, from Ubayy, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-'Adiyat will be given the reward of ten good deeds, equal to the number of those who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed the gathering (jam')" [235].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the racers, panting,﴾ Ibn Abbas, Ata, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi', Atiyyah, Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Kaysan said: They are the horses that run in the way of Allah, and "panting" (ḍabḥ) is the sound of their breaths when they are exhausted in running, so that wheezing increases in their bellies from the intensity of the running. Ibn Abbas said:

"No animal snorts (yaḍuj) except the horse, the dog and the fox."

The lexicographers said: The original meaning of ḍabḥ and ḍibāḥ belongs to foxes, and it was borrowed for horses. It is from the saying of the Arabs: "The fire scorched him (ḍabḥathu) when it changed his color." These animals only pant when their state changes from exhaustion, fear or greed. The word ḍabḥan is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its sense is: "By the racers panting, panting." The poet said:

"You are not an heir of the Yemeni kings if the horses do not pant in the darkness of Iraq [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/154]."

And another said:

"By the racers, the trails of blood upon them, as though their necks were stones of sacrifice set up for worship (tarjib)." [The verse is by Salamah ibn Jandal. al-Asabi means the streaks of blood; asabi al-dima' are its streaks; al-tarjib is the prop for a tree when it bears much fruit.] [Lisan al-Arab: 1/413.]

He means horses.

Muqatil said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyyah) to a clan of Kinanah and appointed over them al-Mundhir ibn Amr al-Ansari, one of the nuqaba'. Their news was delayed, and the hypocrites said: "They have all been killed." So Allah informed him about them, saying: ﴿By the racers, panting﴾, meaning those horses ran until they panted, a sound that is neither neighing (sahil) nor humhama. The wise men said: It is the rattling of rats in hemp. It was said: It is the sound of their lips loosening when they run. Abu al-Duha said: Ibn Abbas used to say: their panting is "aj aj." Others said: They are camels.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed me, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'id informed us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah related to us, saying: Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid related to us, from Abu Salih, concerning His saying: ﴿By the racers, panting﴾. He said: What did Ikrimah see in it? Ikrimah said: Ibn Abbas said: They are horses in battle. I said: (Ali said: They are camels in the Hajj), and I said: "My master knows better than your master."

Al-Sha'bi said: Ali disputed with Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿By the racers, panting﴾. Ibn Abbas said: They are horses. Do you not see that He says: ﴿and raise thereby dust﴾, and can only horses raise dust with their hooves? And do camels pant? Only horses pant. Ali said: "It is not as you say. We saw ourselves on the day of Badr, and with us there was only a dappled horse belonging to al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad."

In another narration: "and a horse belonging to Murthid ibn Abi Murthid al-Ghanawi."

Aqil ibn Abi al-Faraj informed me, from Abu Jarir, who said: Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Abu Sakhr related to us, from Abu Lahi'ah al-Bajali, from Sa'id ibn Husayn, from Ibn Abbas, who narrated to him, saying:

"While I was sitting in al-Hijr, a man came to me and asked about ﴿al-'Adiyat ḍabḥan﴾. I said to him: They are horses when they raid in the way of Allah, then they come back at night and prepare their food and kindle their fire." He turned away from me and went to Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was under the water-vessel of Zamzam, and asked him about ﴿al-'Adiyat ḍabḥan﴾. Ali said: "Have you asked anyone before me?"

He said: "Yes, I asked Ibn Abbas, and he said: They are horses that raid in the way of Allah." Ali said: "Go and call him to me." When he stood over his head, Ali said: "You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of. By Allah, the first battle in Islam was Badr, and with us there were only two horses: a horse for al-Zubayr and a horse for al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. How then can the 'Adiyat be horses? Ibn Abbas said: "I withdrew from my opinion and returned to what Ali said." And to the opinion of Ali went Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad ibn Umayr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi.

Some of them said: Whoever says they are camels takes ḍabḥan to mean ḍab'an, stretching their necks in travel; ḍabaḥat and ḍaba'at have the same meaning. Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib said:

"No, by the racers on the morning of the gathering, with their hooves, when the dust rises."

﴿Then those who strike sparks, striking﴾ Ikrimah, Ata and al-Dahhak said: They are horses that strike fire with their hooves when they travel over stones and stony ground.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: The Arabs call that fire "the fire of Abu Habahib."

Abu Habahib was an old man of Mudar in the pre-Islamic era, and he was among the most miserly of people. He would not kindle a fire for baking bread or for anything else until everyone with an eye had gone to sleep. When his companions slept, he kindled a small fire that flared once and died down once. If anyone woke up and saw it, he extinguished it, out of dislike that anyone should benefit from it. So the Arabs compared this fire to his fire, meaning it benefits no one, just as no one benefits from the fire of Abu Habahib.

The meaning of the verse is: ﴿and the strikers of sparks, striking﴾, thus differing between the subject (sadr) and the verbal noun (maṣdar).

Qatadah said: They are horses that stir up for war, and the fire of enmity between their riders and their knights.

Sa'id ibn Hasan related from Ibn Abbas, who said: They are horses that raid in the way of Allah, then return at night and prepare their food and kindle their fire.

Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam said: They are the deceit of a man. The Arabs say: when a man wants to deceive his companion, he says: "By Allah, I will strike for you and then kindle for you."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They are the men of war. Ikrimah said: They are the tongues of men that kindle fire by what great things they speak.

Ibn Jurayj, from some of them: ﴿al-munjihat 'amalan﴾ are those that succeed in deeds, like the success of the peg when it is struck. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: They are the fires at Jam'.

﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾, meaning the horses, which charge with their riders against the enemy at the time of dawn. This is the view of most exegetes.

Al-Qurazi said: They are camels, pushed by their riders on the day of sacrifice from Jam' to Mina, and the Sunnah is not to push on until dawn. Al-Ighara is swiftness of travel, and from it comes their saying: "Thabir has dawned, as we raided."

﴿Then they raise thereby dust﴾, meaning they stir it up. Abu Haywah read "fa-atharna" with shaddah, from ta'thir. ﴿thereby﴾, that is, at that place which they reached, is a metonymy for something unmentioned, since the meaning is well known and understood.

﴿dust﴾, that is, dust clouds. ﴿and then penetrate thereby into the midst﴾, that is, they enter with it into the midst of them. It is said: wasatu al-qawm (without shaddah) and wassatuhum (with shaddah), and tawassatuhum all have the same meaning. Qatadah read "fa-wassatna" with shaddah. ﴿a gathering﴾, that is, the gathering of the enemy, which is the battalion. Al-Qurazi said: It means the gathering of Mina.

Al-Kalbi said: "In the dialect of Kindah and Hadramawt, and in the dialect of Ma'add all of them, it means: disobedient. In the dialect of Mudar, Rabi'ah and Qada'ah, it means: ungrateful. In the dialect of Banu Malik, it means: stingy."

Shu'bah narrated from Simak that he said: "Kindah was only so named because it cut off its father."

Ibn Sirin said: "It is the one who blames his Lord." Al-Hasan said: "It is the one who counts calamities and forgets blessings." A poet took this up and said:

O you who wrong in his deed,
and wrong returns upon the one who wrongs,
how long will you be, and until when,
complaining of misfortunes and forgetting blessings?
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/160, at the verse.]]

Abu al-Qamar ibn Habib informed us, in Safar of the year 388 (AH), saying: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Sa'd al-Razi informed us, saying: al-'Abbas ibn Hamzah narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying:

Salih ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us from Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, from al-Qummi, from Abu Umamah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), regarding this verse: ﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Do you know what al-kanud is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Al-kanud [he said: it is the ungrateful one who] eats alone, withholds his gift, and beats his servant."
[[Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/384, and Kanz al-'Ummal: 2/48, no. 3064.]]

'Ata' said: "Al-kanud is the one who does not give during a calamity along with his people." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "It is one of little good. And a kanud land is one that grows nothing." Abu Dhubyan said:

Indeed my soul, and I have not been content with you,
but I am afflicted by a kanud age.
[[Fath al-Qadir: 5/483, with variation.]]

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Al-kanud is one whom a single act of kindness has caused to forget many acts of harm."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "Al-kanud is one who sees the blessing as coming from himself and his helpers." Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Tirmidhi said: "It is one who sees the blessing but does not see the Benefactor." Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said: "It is one who spends the blessings of Allah, glorified is He, in acts of disobedience to Allah." Bassam ibn 'Abd Allah said: "It is one who disputes with his Lord over the exchange of reward." Dhu al-Nun: the explanation of "al-halu'" and "al-kanud" is His saying: ﴿When evil touches him, he is anxious; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 20–21].

It has also been said: it is one who disbelieves at little and does not thank for much. It has been said: it is the spiteful. It has been said: it is the envious. It has been said: one who is ignorant of his own worth; and in wisdom, ignorance of one's worth is the tearing away of one's veil. Some of them and al-Hasan said: "His head is on the pillow of blessing, and his heart is in the field of heedlessness." It has been said: he sees what comes from him but does not see what comes to him. The plural of kanud is kund. Al-A'sha said:

He renewed for her, to join you, that she
is a kund for the joining of the frequent visitor.
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/353.]]

I see death seizing the noble and choosing
the prized wealth of the vile, the stingy one.
[[Lisan al-'Arab: 3/234.]]

Al-fahish also means the stingy. Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And he commands you to al-fahsha'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268], meaning stinginess. It has also been said: the meaning is "and indeed he, for love of good, is strong."

﴿Indeed their Lord, concerning them﴾: the plural pronoun is used because "al-insan" is a collective noun.

﴿On that day, is fully Aware﴾: meaning, knowing. The reading is with a kasra on the alif because of the lām; without it, it would be fatḥa, since the knowing would fall upon it. It is not evil in the sight of Allah, but Allah named it evil because people name it evil."

The meaning of the verse: "And indeed he, out of love of wealth, is intensely stingy." It is said of the miser: "shadid" and "mutashaddid." Tarafah said:

I see death seizing the noble and choosing
the prized wealth of the vile, the stingy one.
[[Lisan al-'Arab: 3/234.]]

Al-fahish also means the stingy. Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And he commands you to al-fahsha'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268], meaning stinginess. It has also been said: the meaning is "and indeed he, for love of good, is strong."

Al-Farra' said: the place of "hubb" should be after "shadid," and "shadid" should be added to it, so one would say: "and indeed he is intensely loving of the good." But when "hubb" was placed before "shadid," and the last word was dropped because its mention had preceded, and for the sake of the verse endings, like His saying: ﴿on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18]—stormy (ʿāṣif) does not apply to days but only to wind; and since the mention of wind preceded "day," it was dropped from the end, as if it were said: "on a stormy-wind day."

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾: "scattered" (bu'thira) means overturned and stirred up. Al-Farra' said: "I heard some Bedouins of Banu Asad recite 'buhthira' with a ḥāʾ, and they said: both are dialects."

﴿And what is in the breasts is made apparent﴾: meaning what is in them of good or evil is distinguished and brought out. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read ﴿huṣṣila﴾ with a fatha on the ḥāʾ and a light ṣād, meaning "appeared."

﴿Indeed their Lord, concerning them﴾: the plural pronoun is used because "al-insan" is a collective noun.

﴿On that day, is fully Aware﴾: meaning, knowing. The reading is with a kasra on the alif because of the lām; without it, it would be fatḥa, since the knowing would fall upon it. It has reached me that al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf recited this surah from the pulpit, exhorting people to raid, and on his tongue came: "anna rabbahum" with a fatḥa on the alif; then he corrected it grammatically, saying: "khabīr," and dropped the lām.
